questions.q: Which organisation defines resilience as the 'ability to resist, absorb, recover from or successfully adapt to adversity or a change in conditions'?
questions.e: This is the US DHS definition. Oxford: 'capacity to recover quickly from difficulties'. The Australian paper adds the idea of bouncing *forward*.

questions.q: The Australian Government position paper describes 4 levels of effort in organisational resilience. Which is the highest/most desirable level?
questions.e: Decline → Survive → Bounce Back → Bounce Forward. Adversity can be used to achieve positive change (bounce forward), not just recovery.

questions.q: Resilience is the same thing as cyber security.
questions.e: Cyber security contributes to resilience, but resilience is much broader. Good security can stop cyber attacks, but it cannot stop a typhoon.

questions.q: Per the lecture, resilience is a capability for an organisation to do all of the following EXCEPT:
o: Absorb damages and bounce back to operation
questions.e: Resilience = anticipate adverse events, deal with unknown threats/risks, absorb damage & bounce back, adapt to changes — i.e. continuing existence and staying relevant. You cannot eliminate all adverse events.

questions.q: The 'CEO Perspectives on Organisational Resilience' paper (Australian Attorney-General's Department, 2012) was based on interviews with roughly how many CEOs?
questions.e: It summarised interviews with more than 50 CEOs of Australian organisations.

questions.q: In the CEO Perspectives paper, which resilience concept belongs to the LONG-TERM time horizon?
o: Ability to actively shape the environment of the organisation
Ability to respond to short-term shocks
questions.e: Short term: effective BAU + ability to change & adapt. Long term: actively shaping the environment (innovation, influencing regulation, reinventing the industry — repeatedly).

questions.q: Which concept did NO CEO advocate as ideal, with the vast majority seeing it only as a first step?
questions.e: Highly fine-tuned BAU operations, taken to the extreme, can be very vulnerable to disruptions.

questions.q: Which resilience concept did EVERY CEO see as fundamental?
o: Ability to change and adapt (proactively responding to disruptions)
questions.e: Proactively responding to disruptions was seen by every CEO as fundamental — emphasis on cultures that adapt and support preparedness for shocks.

questions.q: Singapore's inaugural Cybersecurity Strategy was first published in which year (later updated in 2021)?
questions.e: First published by CSA in 2016 and updated in 2021.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the 3 pillars of the Singapore Cybersecurity Strategy 2021?
o: Grow a Robust Cyber Talent Pipeline
questions.e: 'Develop a Vibrant Cybersecurity Ecosystem' and 'Grow a Robust Cyber Talent Pipeline' are the 2 **foundational enablers**, not pillars.

questions.q: How many critical sectors does Singapore identify for Critical Information Infrastructure (CII)?
questions.e: 11 sectors: Energy, Water, Banking & Finance, Healthcare, Transport (Land, Maritime, Aviation), Government, Infocomm, Media, Security & Emergency Services.

questions.q: In which section of Singapore's Cybersecurity Act is a Critical Information Infrastructure (CII) formally defined?
questions.e: Section 7(1): a computer/computer system located wholly or partly in Singapore, necessary for continuous delivery of an essential service, whose loss would have a debilitating effect on that service.

questions.q: Which agency is the sector lead for Singapore's Banking & Finance sector?
questions.e: CSA works with sector leads to identify CII; MAS leads banking & finance (e.g. MAS TRM guidelines apply).

questions.q: Per the NIST ITL Bulletin (July 2010), interim measures to recover after a disruption include all EXCEPT:
o: Paying the attacker to restore system access
Relocating systems and operations to an alternate site
Replacing system functions with manual methods
questions.e: The three interim measures are: alternate site relocation, alternate equipment, and manual methods.

questions.q: What is the FIRST step of the NIST contingency planning lifecycle shown in L01?
questions.e: Policy → BIA → Preventive controls → Contingency strategies → Develop the plan → Testing, training & exercises → Plan maintenance.

questions.q: Which plan, per the L01 outline, typically contains 'Recovery phases', 'Procedures' and 'Testing' sections and lists in-scope applications with their service/application owners?
questions.e: The DRP is the detailed document to recover IT services. The BCP instead has Business sections (BIA, loss scenarios, strategies) and Methodology (incident mgmt, communication).

questions.q: A Critical Infrastructure Protection (CIP) plan is typically owned by a private organisation.
questions.e: A CIP plan is owned by a government (e.g. state/provincial), has general and sector-specific approaches, and uses colour-coded threat levels. Organisations should align their BCP/DRP with it.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the crisis communication principles in L01?
o: Speculate on likely causes to reassure the public
Provide factual facts at that point of time
questions.e: Principles: no lie nor deny, give facts at that point in time, do NOT speculate or forecast, prepare statements, acceptable attitude.

questions.q: In the NIST SP 800-61 incident response lifecycle, which phase is a prerequisite without which the other phases will not exist?
questions.e: Preparation is the prerequisite phase.

questions.q: Which item belongs to the 'Business' part of a typical BCP (per L01)?
questions.e: BCP 'Business' part: BIA, business loss scenarios, BC strategies & requirements. Author/version are 'Information'; org structure is 'Data'.

questions.q: Which source defines a threat simply as 'anything that can result in harm'?
questions.e: ISO 27000: 'potential cause of an unwanted incident, which may result in harm to a system or organisation'. NICCS: 'a circumstance or event that has or indicates the potential to exploit vulnerabilities...'.

questions.q: ISO 27000:2016 defines risk as:
o: The combination of the probability of an event and its consequence
A weakness in an asset or group of assets
Anything that can result in harm
questions.e: ISACA: probability × consequence. NICCS: likelihood that a threat will exploit a vulnerability, with associated consequences.

questions.q: 'A weakness in an asset or group of assets that could allow it to be exploited and harmed by one or more threats' defines a:
questions.e: ISO 73:2009 definition of vulnerability.

questions.q: In the risk relationship model, threats ______ vulnerabilities, and controls ______ risk.
questions.e: Threats exploit vulnerabilities → risk to assets; controls reduce risk.

questions.q: 'Antiquated or outdated technologies' falls under which threat category?
questions.e: Category 12 — Technological obsolescence.

questions.q: Power and WAN issues fall under which threat category?
o: Deviations in quality of service from service provider
questions.e: Category 8 — deviations in QoS from service providers (e.g. power, WAN).

questions.q: Blackmail threatening disclosure of information is an example of:
o: Deliberate acts of espionage or trespass
questions.e: Category 4 — information extortion.

questions.q: What is the main method to protect INTEGRITY of information?
o: Checksum/hash, optionally protected by a digital signature
questions.e: Confidentiality → encryption. Integrity → hash/checksum (+ digital signature). Availability → HA design, no SPOF.

questions.q: The main approach to protecting AVAILABILITY is high-availability design that avoids a ______.
questions.e: Avoid single points of failure (SPOF), end-to-end from server to client.

questions.q: 'The risk of loss resulting from inadequate or failed internal processes, people and systems or from external events' defines:
questions.e: Basel/BCBS definition of operational risk (Principles for the Sound Management of Operational Risk, 2011).

questions.q: The Institute of Internal Auditors (IIA) defines fraud as any illegal act characterised by:
o: Deceit, concealment, or violation of trust
questions.e: Fraud is intentional — deceit, concealment or violation of trust, for financial/property/service gain or advantage.

questions.q: Identity management risks revolve around which three trigger points (plus ongoing BAU)?
questions.e: Joiner–mover–leaver. Threats include account/password sharing, unauthorised usage, weak password policy.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the WEF Global Risks Report risk categories?
questions.e: Five categories: Economic, Environmental, Geopolitical, Societal, Technological.

questions.q: The 2026 Verizon DBIR (19th edition) analysed roughly how many incidents and confirmed breaches?
questions.e: Over 31k incidents with 22k confirmed breaches — the highest number ever analysed in the report.

questions.q: Which DBIR incident classification pattern is #1 in the 2026 report?
questions.e: System Intrusion (61% of breaches in 2026, up from 53%), largely driven by ransomware.

questions.q: Which DBIR pattern is described as 'get in, get the data and get out'?
questions.e: Basic Web Application Attacks — after the initial compromise, few additional actions.

questions.q: In DBIR, lost devices are counted under the 'Miscellaneous Errors' pattern.
questions.e: Misc. Errors covers unintentional actions that compromise a security attribute, but lost devices are grouped with **theft** instead.

questions.q: Per the DBIR 2026 slide, what share of actors were external, and what was the top motive?
questions.e: Actors: external 88%, internal 12%. Motives: financial 88%, espionage 13%.

questions.q: In DBIR terminology, a 'breach' is:
o: An incident that results in confirmed disclosure of data to an unauthorised party
Any security event that compromises CIA
Any observable occurrence in a system
questions.e: Incident = event compromising CIA; breach = incident with CONFIRMED disclosure (not just potential exposure).

questions.q: How many top-level controls are in CIS Controls v8?
questions.e: 18 controls, each with Safeguards; 3 Implementation Groups (IG1–IG3).

questions.q: CIS Implementation Group 1 (IG1) is intended for:
questions.e: IG1: SMEs, limited expertise. IG2: all-purpose cybersecurity. IG3: specialised roles. Each IG builds on the previous one.

questions.q: CIS Control 1 (Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets) contains how many safeguards?
questions.e: Control 1 has 5 safeguards; Safeguard 1.1 is 'Establish and Maintain Detailed Enterprise Asset Inventory'.

questions.q: The 2018 SingHealth cyber attack — Singapore's worst at the time — stole personal info of about how many patients?
questions.e: 1.5 million SingHealth patients (including PM Lee). 665k = MBS 2023; 76m households = JP Morgan 2014; 250m = Microsoft 2020.

questions.q: The November 2023 Marina Bay Sands breach affected about how many non-casino loyalty-programme members?
questions.e: About 665,000 Sands LifeStyle members (names, emails, phone numbers, country, membership number & tier).

questions.q: Which DBIR-recommended CIS Controls apply to System Intrusion? (tick all that apply)
questions.e: DBIR lists: Secure Configuration, Email & Web Browser Protections, Malware Defences, Continuous Vulnerability Mgmt, Data Recovery, Account Mgmt, Access Control Mgmt, Security Awareness & Skills Training.

questions.q: Which BCM definition emphasises 'ensuring uninterrupted availability of all key business resources required to support critical business activities, whether manual or IT-enabled'?
questions.e: ISACA. BS 25999-1: 'holistic management process that identifies potential threats...'. SANS: 'activities required to keep your organisation running during a period of displacement or interruption'.

questions.q: Per Andrew Hiles, BCM is a ______-owned, ______-driven process.
questions.e: BCM is business-owned and business-driven — it is NOT an IT-only exercise.

questions.q: What is the SECOND stage of the BCM lifecycle (Hiles)?
questions.e: 1 Understand the organisation → 2 Determine strategy → 3 Develop & implement response → 4 Exercise, maintain & review → repeat (like PDCA).

questions.q: Which statement about ISO 22301 and ISO 22313 is correct?
o: ISO 22301 is certifiable (the 'what'); ISO 22313 is guidance (the 'how')
ISO 22313 is certifiable; ISO 22301 is guidance
questions.e: Analogous to ISO 27001 (certifiable requirements) and ISO 27002 (guidance). Both were first published in 2012, heavily based on BS 25999.

questions.q: ISO 22301 follows which management model?
questions.e: ISO 22301 BCMS follows the PDCA model.

questions.q: Which ISO 22301 clause is the 'Do' component, covering risk assessment and BIA?
questions.e: Clauses 4–7 = Plan; 8 = Do (operation: BIA, risk assessment...); 9 = Check (performance evaluation); 10 = Act (improvement).

questions.q: Which ISO 22301 clause covers top management's role and the policy statement?
questions.e: Clause 5 — Leadership: what top management should do and what the policy looks like.

questions.q: A BCM policy is an example of a technical control.
questions.e: A policy is an **administrative** control and an enabler that influences all others.

questions.q: Which is NOT listed as a factor influencing a BCM policy?
questions.e: Factors: industry, public vs private, size, jurisdiction, risk appetite & tolerance, attitude to risk, costs. There is no one-size-fits-all policy.

questions.q: A programme consists of two or more projects.
questions.e: BCM is enterprise-wide and complex, so it is run as a programme broken into projects.

questions.q: Step 1 of BCM programme management — establishing governance — starts with:
o: Appointing a senior executive accountable for BCM policy and implementation
questions.e: Appoint a senior executive (CEO/COO etc.), then a subject matter expert (e.g. Head of BC), staff augmentation, then governance/management/support teams.

questions.q: Which statement about the Business Impact Analysis (BIA) is FALSE?
o: All systems and applications have the same importance to continuity
It can use quantitative, qualitative or hybrid approaches
It helps understand dependencies between systems
It influences metrics such as RTO and RPO
questions.e: The whole point of a BIA is that systems are NOT equally important — it categorises and ranks them.

questions.q: For a Cat 1/A (high criticality) system:
o: Downtime is not tolerable or must be very minimal
Some downtime is acceptable within risk appetite
It is excluded from the BCP
questions.e: Cat 1/A severely impacts primary functions; Cat 2/B can afford a period within risk appetite; Cat 3/C minimal impact.

questions.q: Per L03, why is training needed in addition to awareness?
o: Awareness is a starting point but does not provide knowledge acquisition
Awareness is only for external parties
Training replaces the need for exercises
questions.e: Communicate → Training → Exercise. Awareness alone does not build knowledge; exercises test people, processes and tools.

questions.q: What is often the MOST challenging task in BCM programme management?
o: Maintaining the BCM plan so it remains relevant and effective
Writing the first draft of the BCP
questions.e: Maintenance — regular review for changes in strategy/market/socio-political situation, awareness, testing, exercises, monitoring, cost efficiency.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the 6 organisational resources to consider when developing BCM strategies?
questions.e: People, Premises, Technology, Information, Supplies, Stakeholders.

questions.q: Agreeing roles & responsibilities using a RACI matrix is an activity under which organisational resource?
questions.e: Stakeholders: identify stakeholders, communication needs/channels/frequency, RACI matrix, service levels.

questions.q: For the 'Information' resource, beyond CIA, the lecture adds the need to determine the information's:
questions.e: 'Determine the need for Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability and Currency'.

questions.q: Which are the three BCM programme outcomes listed in L03?
questions.e: Discovery (identify key products/risks), Development (processes, people, tools), Compliance (regulators, reputation).

questions.q: Which of these is a benefit of BCM listed in L03?
o: Breaks silos and encourages an enterprise governance approach
questions.e: Benefits: prevents issues, reduces impact/risk to acceptable level, breaks silos, creates competitive advantage.

questions.q: A reliable system is always resilient.
questions.e: They are not the same. Resiliency (ISACA) = ability to resist failure or recover quickly; reliability = consistency of results. A reliable system may not be resilient and vice versa.

questions.q: Recovery Time Objective (RTO) is:
o: The target duration of time to recover a specific business function
The maximum tolerable period in which data might be lost
The longest disruption before organisational survival is threatened
The time to verify data after systems are restored
questions.e: RTO = target recovery duration. RPO = max tolerable data-loss period. MTD = survival threshold. WRT = work recovery time.

questions.q: A system has an RPO of 4 hours. What does this imply?
o: Backups must be taken at least every 4 hours
The system must be back up within 4 hours
Work recovery must take under 4 hours
questions.e: RPO drives backup frequency.

questions.q: Lowering the RTO generally ______ the cost and effort.
questions.e: Quicker recovery requires more resources — determining RTO is a balancing act between business needs and cost.

questions.q: Based on the MTD/RTO/WRT diagram, which relationship holds?
questions.e: MTD is the total tolerable downtime = time to recover systems (RTO) + time to recover work/verify data (WRT).

questions.q: Maximum Tolerable Downtime (MTD) refers to:
o: The longest disruption before the survivability of the organisation is seriously threatened
The target time to restore a system
questions.e: MTD — beyond this point the organisation's survival is at serious risk.

questions.q: On what date did the SGX outage case study occur?
questions.e: SGX went down for almost a day on 5 Nov 2014 (Straits Times report 25 June 2015).

questions.q: What triggered the SGX 2014 outage?
o: A voltage sag in both power lines, plus a malfunctioning component in the backup generator
questions.e: Voltage sag → backup power component malfunction → downstream switches could not cope → momentary total power loss shut down all systems at the primary data centre.

questions.q: Why did SGX initially recover at the primary data centre instead of switching to the backup centre?
o: It was told only a partial power outage had occurred, and internal communication was delayed
The backup data centre was also down
questions.e: At 2.32pm SGX was told only one of two power sources was down; the total outage info only reached the CMT at 3.30pm.

questions.q: SGX: incident at 2.18pm; securities market system recovered at 4.30pm; securities trading resumed at 5.00pm. What were the RTO and WRT for securities?
SGX: incident at 2.18pm; derivatives system recovered at 5.38pm; derivatives trading resumed at 7.00pm. What were the RTO and WRT for derivatives?
In the BCM response timeline, what comes FIRST?
questions.e: Detect & validate → initial response actions → contain → restore to normalcy → communicate.

questions.q: Which exercise type is the most realistic for the WHOLE organisation?
questions.e: Full-scale is the top/most realistic; functional involves intentional failure of a function.

questions.q: Seminars provide affordable access to ______, but not ______.
questions.e: Seminars give knowledge, not concrete skill acquisition.

questions.q: Recommended frequency for FULL-SCALE exercises:
questions.e: Full-scale: every few years. Functional/drills/table-top: once a year. Workshops/seminars: multiple times a year.

questions.q: BCP exercises should be used to assign blame when a deficiency is found.
questions.e: Exercises should be treated as improvement opportunities, not blame-finding.

questions.q: In the BCM verification process, an AUDIT is:
o: Conducted by independent parties and checklist/compliance oriented
Conducted by the first line of defence to find improvements
Conducted by the second line, free-form with wider scope
questions.e: Review = 1st line (improvements). Assessment = 2nd line (free-form, wider scope). Audit = independent (checklist/compliance).

questions.q: Which BCP definition says it 'depends on the contingency plan for restoration of critical systems'?
questions.e: ISACA. BCI: 'documented procedures that guide organisations to respond, recover, resume and restore...'. NIST: 'procedures for sustaining mission/business operations while recovering from a significant disruption'.

questions.q: NIST SP 800-34 rev 1 defines the DRP as providing procedures for:
o: Relocating information systems to an alternate location
questions.e: DRP (NIST) = relocating information systems to an alternate location.

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes BCP from DRP?
o: BCP is strategic (business operations); DRP is tactical (IT assets)
BCP is tactical; DRP is strategic
Both focus only on IT assets
DRP covers people; BCP covers premises
questions.e: BCP: recover/sustain critical business operations. DRP: recover IT assets that support the BC effort.

questions.q: The 'Exclusions' section of a BCP usually arises from:
o: Lack of time to write the plan
questions.e: Exclusions = areas left out, usually due to risk acceptance and budget; the Recovery Assumptions section relates back to it.

questions.q: Which BCP section typically contains a timeline and is used for reporting the progress of the BC effort?
questions.e: The Recovery Progress Log tracks progress over time for reporting.

questions.q: The BCP Sign-Off section shows that the plan has been approved by:
o: The highest level of authority for BCM
questions.e: Sign-off by the highest BCM authority (author, reviewer and approver with signatures).

questions.q: For the DR lifecycle, this module follows which reference?
o: NIST SP 800-34 IT Contingency Planning Process
questions.e: NIST SP 800-34 Chapter 3 (process) and Chapter 4 (plan development).

questions.q: Which is NOT a typical contingency policy element?
questions.e: Policy elements: version history, roles, scope, resource & training requirements, exercise/testing schedules, maintenance schedule, frequency.

questions.q: Ideally, the contingency policy should be sponsored and approved by:
questions.e: Sponsored by executive management (preferably CEO), with a steering committee representing business units and support functions.

questions.q: What are the three steps of the BIA process (NIST SP 800-34)?
o: Identify critical IT resources → identify disruption impacts & allowable outage times → develop recovery priorities
Identify threats → assess vulnerabilities → calculate risk
questions.e: These three steps are on pg. 16–18 of NIST SP 800-34.

questions.q: Which of these is a PREVENTIVE control?
o: Input validation that blocks unwanted character sets
questions.e: Preventive controls keep errors/irregularities from occurring — input validation, access controls, AV, firewalls, IPS.

questions.q: Preventive controls are identified, selected and implemented through:
questions.e: Common preventive controls: multiple sites, multiple teams, redundant utilities, HA (clustering/failover), backup, administrative & technical controls.

questions.q: A facility with only bare minimum support (space, electricity, connectivity) and no servers is a:
questions.e: Cold site — lowest cost, longest setup time.

questions.q: Which alternate site is a replica/extension of the production network running as a primary system and enables instant failover?
questions.e: Mirror site = instant failover but duplicate cost/effort. A hot site still needs customisation and data restore from backup.

questions.q: Which is TRUE about reciprocal agreements?
o: They are hard to realise and typically require a non-competition relationship
They are the cheapest and easiest option to implement
They are always fully owned by both parties
questions.e: An ideal but hard-to-realise arrangement, documented via SLA/MOU/contract.

questions.q: A key benefit of a LEASED alternate site is:
o: Short-term commitment; OpEx instead of CapEx
Full flexibility with no landlord red tape
questions.e: Leased = OpEx/short-term but restrictions and less flexibility. Fully owned = always available but expensive (CapEx).

questions.q: An in-city alternate site's main disadvantage is that it:
o: Suffers from the same vulnerabilities as the primary site
questions.e: In-city: easy, cheap, single regulation — but shares the same vulnerabilities (e.g. floods, grid failure).

questions.q: What are the three main phases of the DRP structure (NIST SP 800-34)?
questions.e: Plus Plan Appendices.

questions.q: Which is NOT a characteristic of a good call tree?
o: A single designated caller for everyone
No single point of failure (primary and secondary)
questions.e: Good call trees avoid SPOFs, use automation (SMS/IVR), have acknowledgement, dynamic contact updates (HR integration) and multiple channels.

questions.q: Damage assessment is typically performed by:
o: The first responder (designated individual or anyone on site)
questions.e: Done by first responders, ideally trained, using pre-defined qualitative ratings supported by quantitative assessment.

questions.q: Who officially activates the contingency plan by declaring the incident?
questions.e: The CMT declares; senior management may be consulted. Pre-defined thresholds reduce delay.

questions.q: All plan activation criteria must be met before the plan can be activated.
questions.e: Only ONE criterion is needed as a trigger (e.g. a fatal casualty on premises even without a disaster).

questions.q: Recovery operations begin after all of the following EXCEPT:
o: The contingency plan has been activated
questions.e: Recovery begins after activation, damage assessment, personnel notified and teams mobilised. RCA is not a prerequisite.

questions.q: Which phase focuses on returning to normalcy, including shutting down the contingency system?
questions.e: Recovery = 'get things working'. Reconstitution = restore/relocate to the 'new normal', back up data from contingency system, shut it down, return staff.

questions.q: Who does the Plan Coordinator engage to identify changes for plan maintenance?
o: Executive Management Committee, Steering Group, Coordinator Team, Involved Parties
questions.e: These four parties help identify changes from regulators, IT and business.

questions.q: Which version of the plan would typically be given to external service providers and vendors?
questions.e: Full version → key people and coordinators; relevant version → external service providers/vendors.

questions.q: Which are backup considerations listed in L05? (tick all that apply)
questions.e: All four: medium, frequency, location, security.

questions.q: The ENISA Threat Landscape (ETL) top threats are prioritised by:
questions.e: ETL ranks threats by frequency, NOT by impact.

questions.q: The ENISA Threat Landscape report has been published annually since:
questions.e: Annual report since 2012.

questions.q: 'Fileless' attacks are hard to detect because they:
o: Use native tools (e.g. PowerShell, WMI) and run directly in memory
questions.e: They avoid writing malware files, evading detection and complicating forensics.

questions.q: WannaCry is cited as an example of 'click-less' infection because it relied on:
o: Remote exploits rather than user intervention
questions.e: Click-less malware spreads via remote exploits without user action.

questions.q: An attacker observes websites frequently visited by victims and infects those sites with malware. This is:
questions.e: Water-holing (watering hole) attacks are a web-based attack trend.

questions.q: A key mitigation specific to Web APPLICATION attacks (SQLi, XSS) is:
questions.e: Plus secure dev/ops policies, traffic filtering, input verification, regular vuln scanning, bandwidth management.

questions.q: Spear-phishing and whaling illustrate which phishing trend?
o: Attacks have become more targeted and sophisticated
questions.e: Targeted attacks; phishing as the initial infection vector; imposed urgency.

questions.q: How do spammers bypass email filters, per ETL?
o: Sending password-protected archives containing macro-laden Word docs or JavaScript
questions.e: Mitigations: block executables/macros, disable auto-execution, user education, AI-based spam detection.

questions.q: Which threat agent remains the largest group, responsible for at least 2/3 of registered incidents?
questions.e: Cyber criminals — profit-driven, increasingly targeted, selling 'Crime-as-a-Service'.

questions.q: Which threat agent is the third most active, with over 20% of incidents and long use of zero-days?
questions.e: Nation states — funded for espionage or cyber combat; attacks are very hard to identify.

questions.q: Hacktivists mainly concentrate on:
questions.e: Politically motivated, within the top 5 security issues; also use Crime-as-a-Service.

questions.q: Which threat agent is defined by a willingness to use violence and often targets critical infrastructure?
questions.e: Capabilities seen as low; more interested in crypto to hide funds/launder money. Cyber fighters are nationally/religiously motivated.

questions.q: In the ISACA attack attributes model, a 'payload' is:
o: A piece of code that takes advantage of a vulnerability
A path used to gain access to the target
questions.e: Attack vector (path) → Payload (container) → Exploit (code) → Vulnerability (weakness) → Target (asset).

questions.q: In the phishing example of attack attributes, what is the VULNERABILITY being exploited?
questions.e: Vector = email; Payload = phishing message; Exploit = fake URL; Vulnerability = lack of awareness; Target = credentials.

questions.q: A key difference between a virus and a network worm is that a worm:
o: Does not require intervention or execution to replicate
Requires the user to run it
questions.e: Viruses need intervention/execution; worms self-replicate across networks on their own.

questions.q: Which malware hides the existence of other malware by modifying the underlying operating system?
questions.e: Rootkit. A backdoor regains access; a keylogger records keystrokes.

questions.q: Ransomware is also known as:
questions.e: Extortive malware that locks or encrypts data/functions and demands payment.

questions.q: Per ISACA CSX, a DoS attack (vs DDoS) originates from:
questions.e: DoS: an assault from a single source that floods a service with requests.

questions.q: A vulnerability exploited before the vendor is even aware of its existence is a:
questions.e: Zero-day.

questions.q: What is the FIRST step of ISACA's Generalised Attack Process?
questions.e: Recon → Create tools → Deliver → Exploit & compromise → Conduct attack → Achieve results → Maintain presence → Coordinate campaign.

questions.q: Covering tracks, installing a backdoor and evading detection belong to which Generalised Attack Process step?
questions.e: Step 7 — Maintain presence.

questions.q: Launching a DDoS, jamming communications and session hijacking are examples of which step?
questions.e: Step 5 — Conduct an attack (the main attacking step).

questions.q: What is the LAST step of the Generalised Attack Process?
questions.e: Step 8: plan larger-scale attacks involving multiple systems, moving across targets including partners. ('Actions on objectives' is Kill Chain.)

questions.q: Subverting an employee/contractor or dropping thumbdrives belongs to which step?
questions.e: Step 3 — insert and install the tools (send malware, drop USBs, tamper with hardware, compromise service provider...).

questions.q: What are the 4 penetration testing phases in ISACA CSX Fundamentals?
questions.e: Planning → Discovery → Attack (with loop back to Discovery) + Reporting throughout.

questions.q: Which pen-test phase occurs simultaneously with all the other phases?
questions.e: Assessment plan in Planning, logs kept in Discovery/Attack, final report with risk ratings and mitigation.

questions.q: In which pen-test phase is a vulnerability assessment conducted?
questions.e: Discovery: compare scanned services/apps/OS against vulnerability databases.

questions.q: Banner grabbing, WHOIS queries and DNS interrogation are techniques of which phase?
questions.e: Information gathering happens in Discovery.

questions.q: Shodan is mentioned as a tool to:
o: Passively profile exposed systems and services
questions.e: An online Internet infrastructure search tool used in Discovery.

questions.q: In the Planning phase, the scope determines whether the test is internal or external, and the test is approved by:
questions.e: Goals set, scope defined, test approved and documented by management.

questions.q: The Cyber Kill Chain was developed by:
questions.e: Lockheed Martin (Hutchins, 2010) to understand adversary TTPs.

questions.q: How many stages does the Cyber Kill Chain have?
questions.e: Recon, Weaponization, Delivery, Exploitation, Installation, C2, Actions on Objectives.

questions.q: Which Kill Chain stage comes immediately after Delivery?
questions.e: …Delivery → Exploitation → Installation → C2 → Actions on Objectives.

questions.q: Coupling an exploit with a backdoor into a deliverable payload happens in which Kill Chain stage?
questions.e: Weaponization prepares the payload; Delivery transmits it.

questions.q: Stopping an adversary at any single stage of the Kill Chain breaks the chain of attack.
questions.e: That is the core defensive insight of the model.

questions.q: Which is NOT a characteristic of an APT?
questions.e: APTs are well-researched, sophisticated, stealthy and persistent.

questions.q: Why are APTs often not detected by traditional security tools?
o: They use custom/dynamically generated malware not detectable by signatures
questions.e: Stealthy: obfuscation, hiding in out-of-reach places, signature-based tools miss them.

questions.q: What are the 5 main phases of the APT life cycle (ISACA)?
o: Intelligence Gathering, Initial Exploitation, Command & Control, Privilege Escalation, Data Exfiltration
questions.e: These 5 phases break down into 10 stages.

questions.q: In APT stage #8, why do attackers compress and ENCRYPT the gathered data?
o: To hide contents from deep packet inspection and DLP at the boundary
To make the victim pay a ransom
questions.e: Encryption hides archive contents from DPI and data loss prevention controls.

questions.q: In APT stage #3 (establish foothold), what does first-stage malware typically do?
o: Beacon home and download additional (second-stage) functionality
questions.e: It has little malicious functionality but can beacon and download second-stage malware.

questions.q: What is the final (10th) stage of the APT life cycle?
questions.e: The APT seeks to maintain access to the target environment.

questions.q: 'Persistent command and control' in the APT context means control that:
o: Survives a reboot and provides regular connectivity
Is only active during business hours
questions.e: Stage #4 Enable persistence.

questions.q: Per the APT threats/motives table, intelligence agencies are motivated by:
questions.e: Organised crime → money/extortion; terrorists → terror; activists → info/disruption; military → cyber warfare positioning.

questions.q: Which is cited as a classic APT example in L08?
questions.e: Stuxnet, the 2013 South Korea attack and the 2014 Sony hack are cited.

questions.q: How do APTs exfiltrate data if outbound FTP is blocked?
o: Custom data transfer tech on standard and non-standard ports
questions.e: They use FTP if allowed, otherwise custom transfer methods on standard/non-standard ports.

questions.q: NIST SP 800-61r2 defines an EVENT as:
o: Any observable occurrence in a system or network
A violation of computer security policies
questions.e: Examples: boot sequence, system crash, packet flooding.

questions.q: NIST SP 800-61r2 defines an INCIDENT as:
o: A violation or imminent threat of violation of security policies, acceptable use policies or standard security practices
questions.e: Incident implies harm or attempt to harm.

questions.q: You see a Windows Domain Controller log line 'An account failed to log on'. This is classified as:
questions.e: A single failed logon is an observable occurrence (event) — not necessarily a policy violation.

questions.q: What is the greatest justification for having an incident management capability?
questions.e: IR doesn't prevent incidents; it minimises loss/disruption (exposure).

questions.q: Which is NOT a 'peaceful time' service of the IR team?
questions.e: Peaceful time: intrusion detection, advisory distribution, education & awareness, information sharing. Eradication is during an incident.

questions.q: Which is NOT a staffing model option for incident response?
questions.e: Employees, partially outsourced, fully outsourced.

questions.q: Handling and communicating with media is important because (tick all that apply):
o: It is hard to retract information once provided
questions.e: All four are reasons from the L09 quiz.

questions.q: Which document is the foundation of the IR programme and defines which events are considered incidents?
questions.e: Policy: defines incidents, org structure, roles, reporting requirements. Plan: roadmap. Procedures: detailed steps.

questions.q: Which is NOT an element of an IR PLAN?
questions.e: Detailed steps belong in IR procedures. Plan elements: mission, strategies/goals, senior mgmt approval, org approach, communication, metrics, maturity roadmap, fit to organisation.

questions.q: Under MAS requirements, Financial Services Institutions must report serious material incidents within:
questions.e: Within an hour to MAS (per MAS TRM FAQ cited in L09).

questions.q: In which IR team model is each regional manager fully responsible for their own region, typically NOT 24/7 but with standby?
questions.e: Centralised and coordinated models offer global 24/7 coverage.

questions.q: Which IR team model has a global service manager acting as a centre of excellence plus regional managers, with 24/7 coverage?
questions.e: Coordinated: regional + central resources coordinate during incidents.

questions.q: Even if IR is outsourced, the organisation still needs:
questions.e: In case external parties are unavailable.

questions.q: Why is employee morale a consideration in selecting an IR team model?
o: IR is high-concentration and demanding and can burn staff out
questions.e: Burnout risk.

questions.q: Which organisations typically receive voluntary incident reports? (tick all that apply)
questions.e: CERT, ISAC, parent organisations, self-regulating industry associations.

questions.q: NIST SP 800-61 rev 3 was published in April 2025 and aligns IR with:
questions.e: Rev3 positions IR as part of organisation-wide cybersecurity risk management.

questions.q: Which CSF 2.0 function was added (it was not in CSF 1.1)?
questions.e: CSF 2.0 has 6 functions: GV, ID, PR, DE, RS, RC.

questions.q: In rev3's mapping, which CSF functions correspond to 'Preparation'?
questions.e: GV/ID/PR = Preparation; DE/RS/RC = Incident Response; ID (Improvement) = Lessons Learned.

questions.q: Incident management & response is a cross-functional process. Which departments does it involve? (tick all that apply)
questions.e: Also senior mgmt, IT security, IT support, BCP.

questions.q: What are the 4 phases of the NIST SP 800-61r2 IR life cycle?
o: Preparation; Detection & Analysis; Containment, Eradication & Recovery; Post-Incident Activity
Preparation; Identification; Containment; Eradication; Recovery; Lessons Learned
questions.e: The 6-phase list is SANS GCIH.

questions.q: SANS GCIH's IR life cycle has how many phases?
questions.e: Preparation, Identification, Containment, Eradication, Recovery, Lessons Learned.

questions.q: A portable case containing materials needed for an IR investigation is called a:
questions.e: Ready to go at all times; items should not be borrowed from it.

questions.q: Network diagrams, lists of critical assets and current baselines are examples of:
questions.e: War room/secure storage = comms & facilities; forensic workstation = hardware/software; clean OS images = mitigation software.

questions.q: Per L10, who are attributed as the 'weakest link' in preventing incidents?
questions.e: Hence user awareness & training as a prevention activity.

questions.q: A DDoS or brute-force attack falls under which attack vector?
questions.e: Attrition — brute-force methods to degrade/destroy systems or networks.

questions.q: Violation of the organisation's Acceptable Use Policy falls under which attack vector?
questions.e: Improper usage.

questions.q: A newly disclosed vulnerability affecting your systems is a:
questions.e: Precursor = sign an incident MAY occur in future. Indicator = sign an incident IS occurring or has occurred.

questions.q: Multiple failed logins followed by a successful login from an unfamiliar location is a(n):
questions.e: Indicator — it suggests an incident is taking place.

questions.q: An antivirus alert indicating malware infection is an example of:
questions.e: IoA = attack attempted/underway (e.g. IDS buffer overflow attempt). IoC = evidence a system may already be compromised.

questions.q: Using TripWire to derive checksums for critical files is an example of:
questions.e: Profiling measures expected activity so changes are easier to spot.

questions.q: Why should all host clocks be synchronised (e.g. via NTP)?
questions.e: Consistent timestamps make it possible to correlate events across systems.

questions.q: Incident prioritisation is based on which factors?
o: Attacker nationality, time of day, cost
Number of users, OS type, location
questions.e: NIST SP 800-61r2 recommends these three.

questions.q: In NIST recoverability effort categories, 'Supplemented' means:
o: Time to recovery is predictable with additional resources
Time to recovery is predictable with existing resources
Time to recovery is unpredictable; outside help needed
questions.e: Regular → Supplemented → Extended → Not Recoverable.

questions.q: Simply monitoring an attacker on a compromised system (instead of containing) is recommended to gather evidence.
questions.e: NOT recommended — the attacker may use compromised systems to attack others. Redirecting to a sandbox is an option, but consult Legal.

questions.q: Why might shutting down an infected host be a bad containment choice?
o: Some malware resides only in memory and disappears on reboot (evidence lost)
questions.e: Also, some malware wipes/encrypts the disk when it detects network disconnection.

questions.q: For a malware infection, 'reconnect the isolated network back to the corporate network' belongs to:
questions.e: Containment = disconnect segment; Eradication = clean/rebuild PCs; Recovery = reconnect.

questions.q: Recording all incident-handler actions in a logbook supports:
questions.e: See NIST SP 800-86 for evidence preservation.

questions.q: Identifying the attacking host should always be the top priority in IR.
questions.e: It can be a distractor — balance it against time/resources needed to contain, eradicate and recover.

questions.q: After a compromise, what is strongly recommended over 'cleaning' the system?
questions.e: A compromised system is no longer trustworthy.

questions.q: How long should evidence be retained if the attacker will be prosecuted?
o: Until legal actions are completed (may take years)
questions.e: Also consider legal/regulatory data retention requirements.

questions.q: Why notify an ISAC after an incident?
o: To share information and help prevent others in the community from being attacked
Because it is the law enforcement body
questions.e: Regulators → as required by law; law enforcement → legal options; ISAC → community sharing.

questions.q: How do NIST CSF 'elements' (used in SP 800-61r3) differ from CIS Safeguards?
o: CSF elements are outcome-based; CIS Safeguards are action-oriented
CSF elements are action-oriented; CIS Safeguards are outcome-based
CSF elements only apply to OT
questions.e: E.g. DE.CM-03: 'Personnel activity and technology usage are monitored to find potentially adverse events'.

questions.q: The CERT Société Générale IRM (Incident Response Methodologies) provides:
o: Incident-specific cheat sheets, freely available on GitHub
questions.e: Practical operational references for incident handlers in multiple languages.

questions.q: CSA SingCERT's Incident Response Checklist is modelled after:
questions.e: SingCERT also publishes IR playbooks.

questions.q: The Detection & Analysis phase seeks to minimise:
questions.e: Analysing events to identify real incidents while minimising false positives.

questions.q: Which of these should be included in incident documentation? (tick all that apply)
questions.e: Also summary, impact assessment, evidence list and handler comments. Incident data must be safeguarded.

questions.q: In which exercise type do participants DISCUSS their responses to a scenario, with 'injects' building complexity?
questions.e: Table-top exercises (TTX) are discussion-based.

questions.q: Compared to a table-top, a functional exercise:
o: Involves hands-on actions on real systems and is more disruptive but more realistic
questions.e: Tests people, processes and equipment where they normally work. Red/Blue/Purple team exercises are a form of functional exercise.

questions.q: A cyber range typically includes a Learning Management System and a(n) ______ layer that maps curriculum to the underlying IT assets.
questions.e: E.g. translating a data-exfiltration scenario into the range's data/network components.

questions.q: How do red team exercises differ from penetration testing?
o: Red teams exploit multiple systems and avenues, not a single application or system
Red teams only scan for vulnerabilities
Red teams never use social engineering
Pen tests are always more realistic
questions.e: 'Think like an attacker' — the gloves are off.

questions.q: In red team rules of engagement, starting with full information about the environment is called:
questions.e: White box = info given; black box = no information.

questions.q: Which team plays DEFENCE in a cyber exercise?
questions.e: Purple teaming combines red and blue collaboratively.

questions.q: The primary result of a table-top exercise is:
o: A summary with participant feedback, positive observations and improvement areas — not pass/fail
A penalty for the IR team
questions.e: Feedback forms are typically distributed immediately afterwards.

questions.q: How often does L11 suggest performing a TTX to keep awareness refreshed?
questions.e: At least annually, so existing staff are refreshed and new staff are trained.

questions.q: Which are the key stakeholders/entities for a cyber security exercise? (tick all that apply)
questions.e: All four are listed.

questions.q: Customers should be informed of an incident before they hear about it from the media.
questions.e: Pre-defined SOPs on what/how/how often to update customers; the exercise validates them.

questions.q: What is the correct order of the exercise planning meetings?
questions.e: Concept Development → Initial Planning → MSEL Planning → Final Planning.

questions.q: How long before the actual exercise does the Concept Development Meeting (CDM) usually take place?
questions.e: IPM is 2–8 weeks AFTER the CDM; FPM is one month before the exercise.

questions.q: After which meeting should exercise objectives and scenario NOT be significantly modified?
questions.e: The IPM finalises objectives and the scenario.

questions.q: At which meeting do exercise leaders make the final GO/NO GO decision?
questions.e: FPM ~1 month before; no new outcomes or scenario changes allowed.

questions.q: What does MSEL stand for?
questions.e: A chronologically sequenced list of injects and expected actions (aka master inject list).

questions.q: Rules of Engagement (ROE) give the test team:
o: Authority to conduct defined activities without needing additional permissions
questions.e: Detailed guidelines and constraints established before the test; signed by network owner and red team lead at FPM.

questions.q: Which group executes the injects and drives the scenario during the exercise?
questions.e: ECG should not be from the Exercise Body (conflict of interest). The Exercise Body responds to the scenario.

questions.q: Injects serve three primary functions. Which is NOT one of them?
o: Reflecting an incident that prompts players to implement the policy being evaluated
questions.e: Injects drive play; they may speed up/slow down the story or add information/questions.

questions.q: Characteristics of good injects include (tick all that apply):
o: Do not conflict with each other
Mirror the real world as much as possible
Have defined time limits to create pressure
questions.e: All four are recommended.

questions.q: Which document captures the exercise background, scope, objectives, scenario, key findings and recommendations?
questions.e: The AAR also lists participants and survey feedback.

questions.q: Which section of the MAS TRM compliance checklist covers Cyber Security Assessment including cyber exercises?
questions.e: Cited in L11 for the banking & finance regulator.

questions.q: IMDA's Codes of Practice for major ISPs were formulated using which international standard (plus IETF BCPs)?
questions.e: ISO/IEC 27011 is the telecom-sector information security controls standard.

questions.q: OPSEC is a term from which US directive?
questions.e: Also US Army Regulation 530-1 Operations Security.

questions.q: As of 2025, the CISSP domain covering operations is called:
questions.e: Updated from 'Operations Security' to 'Security Operations' effective 15 April 2015.

questions.q: Which is NOT an administrative security control in L12?
questions.e: Admin security: labelling, clearance, SOD, rotation of duties, mandatory leave, NDA, background checks. Degaussing is media sanitisation.

questions.q: In labelling/clearance, ______ have labels and ______ have clearances.
questions.e: Objects (to be protected) have labels; subjects (that want access) have clearances.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the popular government labels mentioned for Singapore?
questions.e: Top Secret, Secret, Confidential, Restricted (and Unclassified).

questions.q: The principle that no single person should have complete control of a sensitive transaction is:
questions.e: Maintains checks and balances among privileged employees.

questions.q: Rotation of duties primarily helps to:
questions.e: Can be a detective or deterrent control.

questions.q: Mandatory leave (forced vacation) is similar to job rotation but usually lasts:
questions.e: Another staff member temporarily takes over the role.

questions.q: Data that persists beyond non-invasive attempts to delete it is called:
questions.e: Deleting a file usually only removes metadata pointers — the data remains recoverable.

questions.q: Degaussing destroys data by:
o: Using an external magnetic field to disrupt magnetisation of the media
Overwriting each bit with new data
questions.e: Effective on magnetic media like HDDs. Wiping = overwriting; physical destruction is the most extreme.

questions.q: Which is the MOST extreme mode of media sanitisation?
questions.e: Physical destruction.

questions.q: Capturing a system's security configuration at a point in time is called:
questions.e: Helpful when responding to potential incidents.

questions.q: Continuity of Operations in OPSEC is mainly concerned with which part of the CIA triad?
questions.e: SLAs, backups, RAID, high availability.

questions.q: Which RAID level provides striping with parity?
questions.e: RAID 0 = striping (no redundancy); RAID 1 = mirroring; RAID 5 = striping with parity.

questions.q: Which high-availability configuration is commonly known as load balancing and is the most costly?
questions.e: Active-Passive = one active, one on hot standby.

questions.q: Regularly reviewing users' access rights and privileges is called:
questions.e: Part of (D) Monitoring. Lack of it leads to dormant/obsolete accounts attackers can exploit.

questions.q: What is the correct order of the 5 access rights administration processes?
o: Enrollment → Identification & Authentication → Authorisation → Monitoring → De-registration
questions.e: (A) On-boarding, (B) I&A, (C) Authorisation, (D) Monitoring, (E) Off-boarding.

questions.q: Users typically must agree to which policy before being granted access rights?
questions.e: The AUP describes permitted uses, activities and consequences of non-compliance.

questions.q: How many Operations Security areas are in ISO 27002:2013 Chapter 12?
questions.e: 12.1–12.7: operational procedures, malware, backup, logging & monitoring, operational software, technical vuln mgmt, IS audit considerations.

questions.q: ISO 27002:2013 control 12.4.4 is about:
questions.e: Clocks synchronised to a single reference time source.

questions.q: ISO 27002:2013 control 12.1.4 requires:
o: Separation of development, testing and operational environments
questions.e: 12.1.1 documented procedures; 12.1.2 change mgmt; 12.1.3 capacity mgmt; 12.1.4 separation of environments.

questions.q: What is the objective of ISO 27002:2013 area 12.7 (Information systems audit considerations)?
o: To minimise the impact of audit activities on operational systems
To record events and generate evidence
To protect against loss of data
To prevent exploitation of technical vulnerabilities
questions.e: 12.4 = record events; 12.3 = loss of data; 12.6 = technical vulnerabilities.

questions.q: A key criticism of ISO 27002 noted in L12 is that it:
o: Does not specify technical details on how/when to implement controls
questions.e: Flexibility leads to inconsistent implementations and makes effectiveness hard to judge.

questions.q: ISO 27002:2022 restructured controls into how many themes, and how many controls?
questions.e: Organisational, People, Physical, Technological. 2013 had 14 domains / 114 controls.

questions.q: In NIST SP 800-53 rev 5, Operations Security is explicitly a control under:
o: SC-38 (and SR-7 for supply chain OPSEC)
questions.e: 800-53r5 has 20 control families.

questions.q: Per NIST SP 800-53r5, what is the FIRST of the five OPSEC steps?
questions.e: Identify critical info → analyse threats → analyse vulnerabilities → assess risks → apply countermeasures.

questions.q: Physically recovering trash to find sensitive information that was not securely destroyed is:
questions.e: Mitigated by shredding and proper destruction.

questions.q: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 (announced in the July 2010 ITL Bulletin) replaced an earlier guide issued in:
questions.e: Rev. 1 updated the 2002 guide by integrating risk management and SDLC considerations into contingency planning.

questions.q: The ITL Bulletin says SP 800-34 Rev. 1 covers contingency planning for which three platform types?
questions.e: Three system platforms: client/server, telecommunications, mainframe.

questions.q: FIPS 199 categorises information systems as which impact levels?
questions.e: Based on potential impact to confidentiality, integrity and availability. SP 800-34 provides plan templates for each level.

questions.q: How many steps are in the NIST SP 800-34 contingency planning process?
questions.e: Policy, BIA, preventive controls, recovery strategies, contingency plan, testing/training/exercises, plan maintenance.

questions.q: Per SP 800-34r1, information systems whose availability is categorised as LOW impact:
o: Do not require alternate processing or storage sites
questions.e: Moderate-impact need only the first system backup control enhancements; high-impact strategies may need high-availability and alternate sites.

questions.q: Which plan focuses on restoring mission essential functions (MEFs) at an alternate site for up to 30 days?
questions.e: COOP is mandated for US federal organisations (HSPD-20/NSPD-51, FCD 1). Non-government organisations typically use BCPs instead.

questions.q: Which plan outlines first-response procedures for occupants in a fire, bomb threat or medical emergency, including shelter-in-place?
questions.e: OEPs are facility-level and executed separately as a first response.

questions.q: How does an Information System Contingency Plan (ISCP) differ from a DRP?
o: ISCP procedures recover a system regardless of site; a DRP is site-specific and moves operations to an alternate location
ISCP is site-specific; DRP is site-agnostic
questions.e: Once the DRP moves a site, each system uses its ISCP to restore, recover and test.

questions.q: A DRP only addresses information system disruptions that require relocation.
questions.e: The DRP applies to major, usually physical disruptions that deny access to the primary facility for an extended period.

questions.q: Per SP 800-34r1, the Cyber Incident Response Plan may be included as an appendix of the:
questions.e: It addresses cyber attacks such as unauthorised access, DoS and malicious code.

questions.q: A crisis communications plan typically designates:
o: Specific individuals as the only authority for answering questions from the public
IT staff to post on social media
questions.e: Only approved statements released by authorised officials; includes press release templates.

questions.q: Per SP 800-34r1, which metric is NOT considered part of the MTD?
questions.e: RPO concerns tolerable data loss, not downtime — 'Unlike RTO, RPO is not considered as part of MTD'.

questions.q: Because the RTO must ensure the MTD is not exceeded, the RTO must normally be ______ than the MTD.
questions.e: Extra reprocessing time must fit within the MTD.

questions.q: Which backup type saves files created or modified since the LAST FULL backup?
questions.e: Incremental = since the last backup of ANY type. Differential restore needs only the full + last differential media.

questions.q: Restoring from INCREMENTAL backups typically requires:
o: The full backup plus every incremental since then
The full backup plus only the last differential
questions.e: Incrementals are fast to take but slower/more complex to restore.

questions.q: Why does SP 800-34 NOT recommend RAID-0 as a data recovery solution?
o: It uses striping only and provides no redundancy
It mirrors data to two drives
It requires a dedicated parity disk
questions.e: RAID-1 (mirroring) and RAID-5 (striping with parity) are the most common for recovery.

questions.q: Which alternate site is the most expensive choice but ensures virtually 100% availability?
questions.e: Mirrored sites are fully redundant with real-time mirroring. Cold sites are the cheapest.

questions.q: Per SP 800-34 rev 0, mobile sites may in many cases be delivered to the desired location within:
questions.e: Self-contained transportable shells custom-fitted with equipment.

questions.q: What are the three phases of an ISCP that govern actions after a disruption?
questions.e: Plus supporting information and appendices.

questions.q: Hot sites are typically staffed:
o: 24 hours a day, 7 days a week
questions.e: Hot sites are sized for system requirements and staffed 24/7.

questions.q: In NIST SP 800-61r2 functional impact categories, 'Medium' means:
o: Lost the ability to provide a critical service to a subset of users
Can still provide all critical services but lost efficiency
No longer able to provide some critical services to any users
questions.e: None → Low (minimal effect) → Medium (critical service lost for a subset) → High (critical services lost for all users).

questions.q: Sensitive PII being accessed or exfiltrated is which information impact category?
questions.e: Proprietary breach = unclassified proprietary info (e.g. PCII). Integrity loss = info changed/deleted.

questions.q: Sensitive data exfiltrated and posted publicly would be rated which recoverability category?
questions.e: Recovery from the incident is not possible.

questions.q: Which is NOT a NIST criterion for choosing a containment strategy?
o: Potential damage to and theft of resources
questions.e: Criteria: damage/theft potential, evidence preservation, service availability, time & resources, effectiveness, duration.

questions.q: Why is a 'delayed containment' strategy dangerous?
o: The attacker could escalate access or compromise other systems
It is illegal in all jurisdictions
questions.e: Delaying containment to monitor the attacker carries significant risk.

questions.q: NIST recommends holding the lessons learned meeting:
o: Within several days of the end of the incident
questions.e: Lessons learned meetings are mandatory for major incidents and optional otherwise.

questions.q: NIST SP 800-61r2 describes which three incident response team structures?
questions.e: Staffing models are separate: employees, partially outsourced, fully outsourced.

questions.q: Why should the team avoid borrowing items from the jump kit?
o: The kit must be ready to go at all times to facilitate faster response
questions.e: The point of a jump kit is speed.

questions.q: Under SP 800-61r2, US federal agencies must report incidents to:
questions.e: Each agency designates a primary and secondary POC with US-CERT.

questions.q: Per NIST, most organisations need incident response staff to be available 24/7.
questions.e: 'The Need for 24/7 Availability' is a key team-model consideration.

questions.q: Chain of custody forms, evidence bags and tags are part of which preparation category?
o: Incident analysis hardware and software (evidence gathering accessories)
questions.e: Used to preserve evidence for possible legal action.

questions.q: ISO 22301 defines 'business continuity' as:
o: Capability of the organisation to continue delivery of products or services at acceptable predefined levels following a disruptive incident
Uninterrupted availability of all IT systems
A plan to relocate systems to an alternate site
The process of analysing activities and the effect of disruption
questions.e: The last option is the definition of business impact analysis.

questions.q: In ISO 22301, the time it would take for adverse impacts to become unacceptable is called:
o: Maximum Tolerable Period of Disruption (MTPD) / Maximum Acceptable Outage (MAO)
questions.e: MTPD and MAO share the same definition.

questions.q: The minimum level of services/products acceptable to the organisation to achieve its business objectives during a disruption is the:
questions.e: Minimum Business Continuity Objective.

questions.q: ISO 22301 notes that the RPO can also be referred to as:
questions.e: RPO = point to which information must be restored for the activity to operate on resumption.

questions.q: The act of declaring that business continuity arrangements need to be put into effect is called:
questions.e: ISO 22301 term 3.23.

questions.q: A pre-arranged understanding between two or more entities to render assistance to each other is a:
o: Memorandum of understanding with a regulator
questions.e: Comparable to the reciprocal agreement concept in L05.

questions.q: ISO 22301 defines 'risk appetite' as:
o: The amount and type of risk an organisation is willing to pursue or retain
The maximum loss an insurer will pay
The effect of uncertainty on objectives
questions.e: 'Effect of uncertainty on objectives' is the definition of risk.

questions.q: Which ISO 22301 clause covers 'Business impact analysis and risk assessment'?
questions.e: Clause 8 Operation: 8.1 planning & control, 8.2 BIA & risk assessment, 8.3 BC strategy, 8.4 BC procedures, 8.5 exercising & testing.

questions.q: Which ISO 22301 clause covers 'Exercising and testing'?
questions.e: 9.1 is monitoring/measurement; clause 10 is improvement.

questions.q: ISO 22301 clause 4.3 deals with:
o: Determining the scope of the BCMS
questions.e: Clause 4 = context of the organisation (4.1 context, 4.2 interested parties, 4.3 scope, 4.4 BCMS).

questions.q: Per ISO 22301, 'corrective action' is action to:
o: Eliminate the cause of a nonconformity and prevent recurrence
questions.e: 'Correction' fixes the nonconformity; 'corrective action' removes its cause.

questions.q: The CCoP for CII (Second Edition) took effect on:
questions.e: First release Sept 2018; Addendum Dec 2019; 2nd Edition 4 July 2022. Issued under section 11(1)(a) of the Cybersecurity Act 2018.

questions.q: For an existing CII, the CCoP 2nd Edition Compliance Date is:
questions.e: For a newly designated CII, 12 months from its Designation Date.

questions.q: How often must a CIIO conduct a penetration test on a CII that is an IT system?
questions.e: OT systems: at least once every 24 months.

questions.q: How often must a CIIO conduct a red teaming or purple teaming attack simulation?
questions.e: Clause 5.16.2 — Adversarial Attack Simulation.

questions.q: How often must a CIIO conduct threat hunting on the CII?
questions.e: Clause 6.3 Threat Hunting.

questions.q: Under CCoP 7.3, scenario-based cybersecurity exercises must test which plans? (tick all that apply)
questions.e: All four, at least once every 12 months.

questions.q: Under CCoP logging requirements, logs must be stored for a minimum of:
o: 12 months after the date of the event
questions.e: Clause 6.1.

questions.q: How often must a CIIO review its BCP and DRP?
questions.e: Clause 8.2.5.

questions.q: Which design principles does the CCoP require CIIOs to adopt? (tick all that apply)
questions.e: Clauses 3.4 and 3.5.

questions.q: The CCoP requires multi-factor authentication for privileged accounts and for establishing remote connections.
questions.e: Clauses 5.3 (privileged access) and 5.7 (remote connection).

questions.q: If an audit finds non-compliance, within what time must the CIIO submit an audit finding remediation plan to the Commissioner?
o: 30 working days from receiving the audit report
questions.e: Clause 2.1.1. The plan details remediation actions and timelines; the CIIO implements it at its own cost.

questions.q: Before implementing any part of a CII on cloud, the completed cybersecurity risk assessment must be submitted to the Commissioner within:
questions.e: Clause 3.7.3 — Use of Cloud Computing Systems and Services.

questions.q: Which section of the CCoP covers Response and Recovery (incident management, crisis communication, exercises)?
questions.e: 5 = Protection; 6 = Detection; 7 = Response & Recovery; 8 = Cyber Resiliency (backup, BCP/DRP); 10 = OT security.

questions.q: The Counter-Ransomware Task Force (CRTF) was chaired by:
o: The Commissioner of Cybersecurity / Chief Executive of CSA
questions.e: Convened January 2022, with CSA, MAS, MHA, SPF, MCI, IMDA, MINDEF, GovTech and AGC support. Report: November 2022.

questions.q: How many times did the CRTF meet between January and September 2022?
questions.e: Three key outcomes: ransomware kill chain, position on paying ransoms, recommended strategies.

questions.q: How many stages are in the CRTF's reference ransomware kill chain?
questions.e: The first three stages happen before ransomware activation; stage 4 encrypts; stage 5 displays the ransom note.

questions.q: According to the CRTF, the priority should be to stop the kill chain at:
questions.e: Prevention is better than cure — e.g. Protective DNS (pDNS) and takedown measures.

questions.q: Singapore's national position on paying ransoms is that payment is:
questions.e: Paying fuels the problem, doesn't guarantee decryption, and may mark you as a 'soft target'.

questions.q: Paying a ransom could, depending on facts, contravene which Singapore Act?
questions.e: CII owners and agencies should notify CSA and SPF immediately before any ransom payment.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the CRTF's four pillars of action?
o: Legalise ransom payments to speed recovery
questions.e: The 4 pillars: strengthen defences, disrupt the business model, support recovery, work with international partners.

questions.q: How many ransomware cases were reported by Singapore companies to SingCERT in 2021?
questions.e: Most, if not all, originated from overseas.

questions.q: In the Ransomware-as-a-Service model, who leverages the service and does the bulk of the work spreading ransomware via attacks?
questions.e: Developers write the ransomware and sell to operators; operators provide RaaS; affiliates spread it, and operators take a cut.

questions.q: Why are decryption keys and backups only partially effective against modern ransomware?
o: Double extortion — attackers also threaten to publish stolen data
questions.e: Data restoration doesn't stop the leak threat.

questions.q: Before Version 8, CIS 'Safeguards' were known as:
questions.e: v8.1.2 has 18 Controls with Safeguards.

questions.q: CIS defines IG1 as:
questions.e: The foundational safeguards every enterprise should apply against the most common attacks.

questions.q: IG3 includes all Safeguards in IG1 and IG2.
questions.e: Each IG builds on the previous one.

questions.q: CIS Controls v8.1 added which new security function, aligning to NIST CSF 2.0?
questions.e: Governance topics are now specifically identified.

questions.q: CIS Implementation Groups were first introduced in which version?
questions.e: Earlier versions referred to the first six controls as 'cyber hygiene', which proved too simplistic.

questions.q: CIS Control 11 is:
questions.e: 10 = Malware Defenses; 8 = Audit Log Management; 18 = Penetration Testing.

questions.q: CIS Control 17 is:
questions.e: 16 = Application Software Security; 15 = Service Provider Mgmt; 13 = Network Monitoring and Defense.

questions.q: Which number is CIS Control 'Security Awareness and Skills Training'?
questions.e: 5 = Account Management; 9 = Email & Web Browser Protections; 12 = Network Infrastructure Management.

questions.q: CIS Control 1 and Control 2 cover inventory and control of:
questions.e: Control 3 = Data Protection; 4 = Secure Configuration.

questions.q: Which CIS Control was the last (18th) control?
questions.e: Control 18: Penetration Testing.

questions.q: In DBIR 2026, which is now the most common initial access vector for breaches?
questions.e: Credential abuse, the previous leader, fell to 13%.

questions.q: What share of critical vulnerabilities in the CISA KEV catalog were fully remediated in 2025, and what was the median time?
questions.e: Down from 38% the previous year; median full resolution rose from 32 to 43 days.

questions.q: Ransomware was present in what share of breaches in DBIR 2026?
questions.e: Up from 44%. 69% of victims didn't pay; median payment fell to $139,875.

questions.q: What share of ransomware victims did NOT pay in DBIR 2026?
questions.e: Ransom payments continue to decline.

questions.q: Breaches with third-party involvement reached what share of total breaches?
questions.e: An increase of 60% from the previous year's dataset.

questions.q: The human element was present in what share of breaches in DBIR 2026?
questions.e: A slight increase from 60%.

questions.q: The DBIR 2026 dataset covers which period and how many countries?
questions.e: Data from almost a hundred contributors, normalised with VERIS.

questions.q: Which framework does DBIR use to normalise incident data?
o: VERIS (Vocabulary for Event Recording and Incident Sharing)
questions.e: VERIS has seven threat action categories: Malware, Hacking, Social, Misuse, Physical, Error, Environmental.

questions.q: Per DBIR, a DDoS attack is most often classified as an incident rather than a breach.
questions.e: Because data is rarely exfiltrated.

questions.q: In DBIR 2026, the median threat actor researched or used AI assistance in how many documented techniques?
questions.e: Some actors leveraged 40–50. Most AI-assisted malware used well-known techniques (median 55 existing malware examples).

questions.q: How is Social Engineering evolving per DBIR 2026?
o: Increasing use of voice and mobile-centric techniques
questions.e: Catching people off guard in the middle of the workday.

questions.q: What is the #1 global risk by severity over the SHORT TERM (2 years) in the WEF Global Risks Report 2026?
questions.e: Top 5 short term: Geoeconomic confrontation, Misinformation & disinformation, Societal polarisation, Extreme weather, State-based armed conflict.

questions.q: What is the #1 global risk over the LONG TERM (10 years)?
questions.e: Top 3 long term: Extreme weather, Biodiversity loss & ecosystem collapse, Critical change to Earth systems.

questions.q: Which risk ranks #2 in the short term?
questions.e: It drops to #4 in the 10-year ranking.

questions.q: Where does 'Cyber insecurity' rank in the short and long term?
questions.e: Technological risks are 'growing, largely unchecked'.

questions.q: Which risk shows the largest rise in ranking over time, moving from #30 (2-year) to #5 (10-year)?
questions.e: Section 2.7 'AI at large' explores its impact on labour markets, societies and information security.

questions.q: The Global Risks Report 2026 is which edition, drawing on over how many experts?
questions.e: The ~11,000 figure refers to business leaders in the separate Executive Opinion Survey.

questions.q: What share of GRPS respondents anticipated a 'calm' global outlook over the 2-year horizon?
questions.e: Only 1%; about 50% anticipate turbulent or stormy conditions in the next two years.

questions.q: How many global risks does the report cover in its rankings?
questions.e: Across five categories: economic, environmental, geopolitical, societal and technological.

questions.q: The Basel definition of operational risk includes ______ risk but excludes ______ risk.
questions.e: 'Risk of loss resulting from inadequate or failed internal processes, people and systems or from external events.'

questions.q: In the three lines of defence model, the FIRST line is:
questions.e: Business lines identify and manage the risks inherent in their products, activities, processes and systems.

questions.q: The SECOND line of defence is typically:
o: A functionally independent corporate operational risk function (CORF)
questions.e: The CORF challenges business lines' inputs/outputs and designs/maintains the framework.

questions.q: The THIRD line of defence is:
questions.e: Reviewers must not be involved in developing, implementing or operating the framework.

questions.q: How many principles are in the BCBS 'Principles for the Sound Management of Operational Risk' (2011), and which one covers business resiliency and continuity plans?
questions.e: Principle 10: banks should have business resiliency and continuity plans to operate on an ongoing basis and limit losses in severe disruption.

questions.q: BCBS Principle 1 states that the board of directors should:
o: Take the lead in establishing a strong risk management culture
Delegate all risk matters to IT
questions.e: Principle 1 — risk culture led by the board.

questions.q: Per the BCBS principles, indicators used to monitor the main drivers of exposure associated with key risks are called:
questions.e: KPIs instead give insight into the status of operational processes. Other tools: internal/external loss data, scenario analysis.

questions.q: In the IMF note's six-step process to develop a BCP/DRP, Step 6 is:
questions.e: 1 Document activities → 2 BIA → 3 Develop BCP/DRP → 4 Implement/update → 5 Training → 6 Regular (annual) testing & updating.

questions.q: Per the IMF note, the cost-vs-recovery-time trade-off is:
o: Non-linear — cost rises sharply as recovery time shrinks from days to minutes
questions.e: Costs rise exponentially if recovery time is reduced to minutes rather than hours/days.

questions.q: The IMF note advises that an alternate site should be:
o: Far enough away (e.g. on a different power grid) so both sites aren't impacted simultaneously
In the same building for convenience
questions.e: Regularly using the alternate site for training is also recommended.

questions.q: Per the IMF note, unlike market or credit risk, operational risk is mainly:
o: Endogenous (internal) to the ministry of finance
questions.e: Apart from external events like natural catastrophes, it is tied to processes, systems, management and information flows.

questions.q: According to FEMA's 'Every Business Should Have a Plan', what is the most common of all business disasters?
questions.e: 'Fire is the most common of all business disasters.'

questions.q: FEMA's Ready Business recommendations reflect which standard?
questions.e: The Emergency Preparedness and Business Continuity Standard developed by the National Fire Protection Association.

questions.q: For succession of management, FEMA recommends including:
o: At least one person who is not at the company headquarters
questions.e: So leadership survives a disaster that hits HQ.

questions.q: FEMA advises businesses to review their plans:
questions.e: Just as your business changes, so should your plan.

questions.q: In the DHS (ready.gov) BCP template, where should multiple print copies of the plan be kept?
questions.e: So team members can quickly review roles and reference info when activated.

questions.q: In the DHS BCP template, which section identifies RTOs and RPOs?
questions.e: BIA: identify RTOs for business processes/IT and RPO for data restoration.

questions.q: Per the SANS 'Introduction to BCP' paper, what is the FIRST BCP phase?
questions.e: Project Initiation → Business Analysis → Design & Development → Implementation → Testing → Maintenance.

questions.q: The SANS BCP paper recommends the coordinator conduct testing with management approval at least:
questions.e: Testing should be designed carefully to avoid disrupting production.

questions.q: What are the four tiers of the SBF/SLA BCM-Readiness Framework for Singapore's logistics sector?
o: Decline, Survive, Bounce Back, Bounce Forward
questions.e: Moving up the tiers = increasing sophistication / BCM maturity.

questions.q: The SBF logistics BCM-Readiness Framework is based on which requirements?
o: The seven requirements of ISO 22301 (Clauses 4 to 10)
questions.e: It also references Singapore's earlier SS 540:2008 BCM standard.

questions.q: In SBF's 2013 BCM survey, nearly what share of respondents had NOT activated their business continuity plan?
questions.e: Motivating the self-assessment/diagnostic tool.

questions.q: In the SBF logistics guide, which body sets directions and corporate objectives and approves the BCM policy?
questions.e: The steering committee provides governance and approval.
